questions.prompt: You list rule one as `{ pattern: /^git\s+push\b/, reason: '...' }` — blocking every push — and keep a `git push --force-with-lease` allow-case test below it. The self-test fails on that allow case. Why?
options: Rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so the broad push rule fires before the `--force-with-lease` exception below it is ever reached
`--force-with-lease` is a different command the `Bash` matcher doesn't cover
The self-test only checks block cases, so the allow case was never actually run
`--force-with-lease` contains `--force`, and no regex can exclude a substring it matches
questions.explanation: The list is scanned with `.find()`, so the first rule whose pattern tests true decides the outcome. A broad rule placed above a narrow exception makes the exception dead code — the safe variant is swallowed before its allow-case can save it. The fix is to put the exclusion inside the rule that actually matches, e.g. `^git\s+push\b(?!.*--force-with-lease)`. Option B is wrong because the matcher fires the script on every Bash command; the script, not the matcher, does the deciding. Option C misses that the test did run — that's how the failure was seen. Option D misreads regex: a negative lookahead excludes exactly that substring, which is the pattern the lesson uses.

questions.prompt: You add a `PostToolUse` hook on `Edit|Write`, intending to block writes to generated files. Its script exits 2 with a clear reason. The agent writes a file under `dist/`. What happens?
options: The write lands; exit 2 on `PostToolUse` sends the reason to the model instead of blocking, so the guardrail must move to `PreToolUse`
The write is refused and the reason is shown as the blocking reason
The write lands, and nothing reaches the model
The write is refused only on the second attempt
questions.explanation: `PostToolUse` cannot block because the tool already ran; exit 2 there is a way to hand the model feedback, which is why the lesson's generated-file hook uses `additionalContext` and deliberately does not try to block. A guardrail — enforcement before the action — belongs on `PreToolUse`. Option B is the exact confusion the event table exists to prevent. Option C undersells it: the reason does reach the model, which is why a wrong-seam hook can look like it is doing something. Option D invents a retry that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: You want a fifth forbidden command. Where does it go, and why does that choice matter?
options: As a new entry in the `BLOCKED_COMMANDS` array — adding data can't introduce a new code path or a new way to fail
As a new `if` branch ahead of the existing ones — more explicit and easier to test
In `CLAUDE.md` beside the other rules, so the model sees it as well
In a second, separate script, so a bug in one can't affect the other
questions.explanation: Policy-as-data is the point: a rule is a line in an array, and adding a line cannot add a branch, a crash surface, or an untested path. Option B is what the array replaced — every new branch is a new way to fail, which is how four copy-pasted scripts drift out of sync. Option C puts enforcement back in the window, where it is a request again. Option D scatters the policy, so nobody can read or update it in one place and you now have several failure surfaces instead of one.

questions.prompt: Your `PreToolUse` guardrail does two regex tests and declares no `timeout`. A typo makes it block on reading stdin forever. What does the user experience?
options: The session can hang for up to 600 seconds — the default command-hook timeout — which is why a fast guardrail sets a short explicit `timeout: 5`
The hook is killed at 30 seconds and the tool call proceeds
`PreToolUse` has no timeout, so the session hangs until it is killed by hand
The harness runs the tool anyway after 10 seconds
questions.explanation: The default timeout for command hooks is 600 seconds — ten minutes — and it exists for slow work, which a two-regex guardrail is not. A bug then becomes a six-hundred-second freeze in your session. Option B quotes 30s, which is the default on some events, not this one. Option C is wrong: a timeout exists, it is just far too generous. Option D misreads the failure path — a timeout doesn't fast-forward the tool.
